name: Sanshan Guowang (Three Mountain Kings)
domain: Protecting the Hakka community, guarding the mountains and forests, blessing farming
description: In Taiwan there's an old rule of thumb for finding a Hakka village: look for a temple to the Three Mountain Kings. The Three Mountain Kings — Sanshan Guowang, also called Guowang Ye or San Wangye — began as the gods of three peaks in Jieyang, Chaozhou, in Guangdong: Jinshan, Mingshan and Dushan. They are often held up as the emblem of Hakka faith. Back in their homeland they belonged to all of Chaozhou's communities; but after the crossing to Taiwan, Hakka settlers worshipped them so devoutly that the Kings became a marker of Hakka settlement — folk wisdom even says, "wherever there's a Sanshan Guowang temple, there are Hakka people." That is only a saying, though: Hoklo people worship the Three Mountain Kings too, and the faith is not exclusively Hakka. For the early Hakka pioneers, the Kings did more than bless the harvest and guard the hills; they were the spiritual backbone that held a community together on unfamiliar ground. Taiwan has more than 200 temples dedicated principally to them, most of all in Yilan, Pingtung and Changhua. Pingtung Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple, built in 1778 (the 43rd year of the Qianlong reign), is a Pingtung County historic site.
story:
Legend says the Three Mountain Kings were once three sworn brothers at the end of the Sui dynasty — the eldest, Lian Jie, King of Jinshan; the second, Zhao Xuan, King of Mingshan; the third, Qiao Jun, King of Dushan — who protected the villagers and drove off bandits in a lawless age. Later, when Emperor Taizong of Song marched against the Northern Han, the three mountain gods appeared to aid his army. For this they were made kings, and the court granted their temple the plaque "Mingkuang." Another account holds that they were simply the nature gods of three mountains, given more and more human form as dynasty after dynasty added to their titles.

But in Taiwan, the Kings' story was written mostly in the sweat and blood of Hakka settlers. In the Qing era, when clashes between immigrant groups were frequent, Hakka settlements were often outnumbered, and the Sanshan Guowang temple was usually the village's main defensive stronghold — where the temple stood, the line held, and that's where the people made their stand. The Kings were more than gods; in turbulent times they were the Hakka answer to "who are we, and what are we defending?"

That is why, whenever Hakka families moved, they first went to the Sanshan Guowang temple to carry incense with them, then built a new temple when they reached their new home. The mountain gods followed the people, and the protection of the homeland never fell away.

temples.name: Xinzhuang Guangfu Temple
temples.deityStory: Built in 1780 (the 45th year of the Qianlong reign) with funds from Xinzhuang's Cantonese immigrants of Chaozhou origin, it is a national historic site. After those immigrants moved away the temple was seldom renovated — which is exactly why it has kept its Qing-dynasty appearance.

temples.name: Xinpu Guanghe Temple
temples.deityStory: Founded in the Xianfeng era of the Qing dynasty by Chaozhou immigrants in Xinpu, it was burned by Japanese troops in 1895 and rebuilt. Inside are koji ceramics signed in 1928 by the Quanzhou master craftsman Su Yang-shui.

temples.name: Pingtung Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple
temples.deityStory: Built in 1778 (the 43rd year of the Qianlong reign) and rebuilt on its present site in 1866 (the 5th year of the Tongzhi reign), it is a Pingtung County historic site. The "Wei Zhen Hai Dong" plaque in the main hall is dated to the very year the temple was built.

associatedTemples: Xinzhuang Guangfu Temple (Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City)
Xinpu Guanghe Temple (Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County)
Pingtung Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple (Jiuru Township, Pingtung County)
worship:
Worship of the Three Mountain Kings keeps many Hakka traditions. Offerings center on the Three Sacrifices (pork, chicken and fish), fruit, tea and wine — with more weight placed on pork than in Hoklo worship. The order matters: offer incense first at the Heaven Censer, then to the First, Second and Third Kings in turn. Sanshan Guowang temples in Hakka villages usually also enshrine Han Wengong (Han Yu) and the local earth god, Bo Gong, so you can pay your respects to them as well.

The Kings' birthday on the 25th day of the 2nd lunar month is the event of the year, marked with Hakka bayin ensemble music and opera performed for the gods. Some temples still choose the year's "censer master" by casting moon blocks, and that person then oversees the year's ceremonies.

Nothing shows the weight of this faith better than an old Hakka custom: before moving house or village, you first go to the Sanshan Guowang temple to carry incense with you, and build a new temple at your new home — the guardian always walks ahead of the family.
festivals: The Kings' Holy Birthday on the 25th day of the 2nd lunar month is the most important festival at Sanshan Guowang temples everywhere, with birthday ceremonies and banquets held at each temple.

name: Yimin Ye (Righteous People Lord)
domain: Defending the homeland, the spirit of loyalty and righteousness, protecting the Hakka community
description: Yimin Ye — also called Yimin Gong, Zhongyi Gong or Baozhong Yimin Ye — are not gods from heaven. They are Hakka militiamen of the Qing dynasty who died defending their homes. During upheavals such as the Zhu Yigui Incident (1721) and the Lin Shuangwen Incident (1786), Hakka settlers organized their own militias to protect their villages and keep order, and many of them fell. Later generations enshrined these self-sacrificing spirits together and honored them as Yimin Ye, the Righteous Martyrs. This is a faith of people who became gods: what devotees worship is not supernatural power, but gratitude and remembrance for forebears who gave their lives for their homeland. The Yimin Festival each seventh lunar month is the grandest religious celebration of Taiwan's Hakka people, hosted in rotation by fifteen great villages of the Taoyuan–Hsinchu region, and in 2015 it was registered as a National Important Folk Custom. For the Hakka it is more than a festival — it is the yearly answer to "where did we come from?"
story:
In 1786 (the 51st year of the Qianlong reign), Lin Shuangwen rose in revolt in Changhua. His forces swelled and chaos spread far and wide. The Hakka settlements around Hsinchu and Taoyuan did not sit and wait: they raised their own volunteer armies to defend their homes and fought through dozens of battles, large and small.

When the fighting was over, the fallen volunteers were buried together at Fangliao (today's Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County), and the villagers built a temple beside the tomb. Emperor Qianlong, praising their loyalty, bestowed two characters — "Baozhong," honoring loyalty — which is why the Fangliao temple's full name is Baozhong Yimin Temple. Volunteers who died in the Dai Chaochun Incident during the Tongzhi era were later buried in an annex grave beside the Yimin Tomb, and the temple became the sacred symbol of the Taiwanese Hakka spirit.

What sets the Yimin temple apart is that the heart of the faith is not a statue but a tomb. The Yimin Tomb behind the temple holds the fallen of successive conflicts, and it remains the center of the whole faith today — devotees are honoring a real grave, with real people resting inside.

Among Taiwan's temples, nothing else is like it. And precisely because of that, the Yimin faith carries not myth but history, written by the Hakka with their own lives: defend the homeland, and put righteousness first.

temples.name: Baozhong Yimin Temple
temples.deityStory: The head temple of Yimin faith in Taiwan. Construction began in 1788 (the 53rd year of the Qianlong reign), and the main hall was completed in 1790. The Yimin Tomb behind the temple holds the martyrs who fell in successive conflicts. The Yimin Festival on the 20th day of the 7th lunar month is hosted in rotation by fifteen great villages and is celebrated on a grand scale; its most distinctive rite is the "Divine Pig Competition," the Hakka's most generous tribute to their forebears.

associatedTemples: Baozhong Yimin Temple (Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County)
worship:
Worshipping Yimin Ye is unlike worship at an ordinary temple. First of all, there is no deity statue — the heart of the faith is the Yimin Tomb behind the temple. Offer incense first before the Yimin Ye's tablet in the main hall, then go around back to pay your respects at the tomb.

Offerings center on the Three Sacrifices and Five Offerings, with pork the most important of all — the Hakka's most generous tribute to their forebears. The best-known tradition is the "Divine Pig Competition": devotees raise huge pigs to offer, villages show them off at each year's Yimin Festival, and the heaviest pig brings its village enormous honor.

There is also a special custom called "feng fan," offering meals: in the month or two before the festival, the villages of the rotating host district bring cooked food to local worship sites and set it before the Yimin Ye's command flag, the way you would serve your own elders. Because to the Hakka, the Yimin Ye were never distant gods in heaven — they are their own ancestors.
festivals: The Yimin Festival on the 20th day of the 7th lunar month is the grandest annual celebration of Taiwan's Hakka people. It is hosted in rotation by fifteen great villages (village alliances) in the Hsinchu and Taoyuan region, each taking one year, for a full cycle of fifteen years. The festivities run for several days, and the core rites include the "Divine Pig Competition" (each village displaying its giant offering pigs), the release of water lanterns (floated down the river to light the way for wandering spirits, the "good brothers"), and a nighttime procession carrying offerings on shoulder poles. The Yimin Festival was registered as a National Important Folk Custom in 2015 and is one of the best ways into Taiwan's Hakka culture.

name: Bo Gong (Earth God)
description: In Hakka villages, the earth god Tudi Gong (Fude Zhengshen) goes by a warmer name — Bo Gong, the way you'd address an uncle in your own family. That familiarity is what makes Hakka faith so touching. There is a Field-Head Bo Gong to watch the crops, a Water-Head Bo Gong by the irrigation channel, a Village-Head Bo Gong guarding the way in and out, a Mountain-Foot Bo Gong protecting the hills — wherever the Hakka go, Bo Gong is there. His "home" comes in any form: a proper temple, a small roadside stone shrine, or even just a "stone shelter" made of three stone slabs. Unlike the gilded earth-god temples of the Hoklo, Hakka Bo Gong shrines often hide under old trees or along the ridges between paddies, so plain they almost melt into the landscape. Meinong District in Kaohsiung alone has nearly 400 Bo Gong altars. The Hakka also developed "zo Bo Gong fuk" — the whole village sharing a meal in front of Bo Gong's shrine, thanking the god and catching up with the neighbors — turning faith into everyday life.
story:
When Hakka pioneers crossed the sea to Taiwan, the first thing they did on newly cleared land often wasn't building a house — it was setting up a Bo Gong altar. Greet the land first; talk about farming it after.

Legend says Bo Gong was once an old man named Zhang Fude, an honest official who loved to help others; after his death, people who remembered his virtue honored him as the god of the land. But in Taiwan, Hakka Bo Gong worship grew into its own shape. Meinong has a rare kind of Bo Gong called "Lishe Zhenguan," which comes from the Qing government's lishe community-altar system. These are mostly set at a water outlet, so they are also called Water-Mouth Bo Gong — and there are only three in all of Taiwan, all of them in Meinong.

From the days of crossing and clearing land until today, Bo Gong has been the most everyday of Hakka gods: never lofty, simply keeping watch at the head of the fields and the end of the water channel, like an elder who is always there.

temples.name: Meinong Kaiji Bo Gong Shrine
temples.deityStory: The earliest Bo Gong altar set up in Meinong's Hakka villages, a witness to the history of how Meinong was settled.

worship:
Worshipping Bo Gong doesn't take much fuss. On ordinary days a plate of fruit and a pot of tea or rice wine is enough; at festivals, add the Three Sacrifices (pork, chicken and fish) and sweet rice cake (nian gao). Hakka tradition is to worship Bo Gong on the 1st and 15th of each lunar month, and devout elders may even light incense every day.

The most Hakka custom of all is "zo Bo Gong fuk" (also called "eating Bo Gong's blessing"): village households take turns preparing food and everyone eats together in front of the shrine — half to thank the god, half to keep neighbors close. This is where Hakka community spirit comes from.

Farmers keep their own calendar too: before the busy season they pray at the Field-Head Bo Gong, and after the harvest they come back to give thanks. The awe and wisdom of people who live by the weather is all there, in that coming and going.
festivals: Bo Gong's Birthday (the earth god's birthday) on the 2nd day of the 2nd lunar month is the most widely observed Bo Gong festival in Hakka villages. Shrines everywhere are hung with lanterns and decorations, devotees bring offerings to wish him long life, and some temples stage Hakka opera or glove puppet shows for the god. Bo Gong is also commonly worshipped at the Mid-Autumn Festival. In spring, Meinong holds its "Second-Month Opera," with performances staged before Bo Gong altars to thank the god.

name: Wugu Shennong Dadi (Divine Farmer Emperor)
domain: Bountiful harvests, medicine and health, safe crops
description: Bare-chested, wearing a skirt of leaves, two horns on his head and a sheaf of rice in his hand — this is the Divine Farmer, Wugu Shennong Dadi, also called Shennong Dadi, the King of the Five Grains, or the King of Medicine. One of the Three Sovereigns of high antiquity, he is the founder of agriculture and medicine. Legend says he tasted hundreds of herbs himself and taught people to farm, making him the spiritual source of a civilization built on agriculture and of the belief that food and medicine share one root. In Taiwan, Shennong is the patron of farmers, herbal medicine merchants, Chinese medicine doctors and cooks alike, and Taiwan's early Wugu (Five Grains) temples were mostly kept by immigrants from Guangdong. For the Hakka, farmers for generations, this "divine farmer" is the founding master of their own trade. His horned headdress is his most recognizable feature — you'll know him at a glance. Every year on his birthday, the 26th day of the 4th lunar month, Shennong temples everywhere hold celebrations, and before spring planting and after the autumn harvest you'll always find farmers in the temple.
story:
"Shennong tastes a hundred herbs" may be the most heroic and tragic tale in all of ancient Chinese myth.

Legend says Shennong was the Flame Emperor, Yandi — the "Yan" in the phrase "descendants of Yan and Huang" that Chinese people use for themselves. To teach people which plants were safe to eat and which could heal, he chose the most direct method there was: he ate them himself. The folk version says he was poisoned seventy-two times in a single day and cured himself with tea leaves — which is where tea's title, "King of a Hundred Herbs," comes from. He passed what he learned on to the people; farming and medicine became separate arts, and the foundations of Chinese medicine were laid.

The last time, he tasted a deadly plant (some say heartbreak grass) whose poison he could not undo, and he died for his calling. An emperor traded his own life for his people's dinner tables and medicine cabinets.

He is also said to have invented the leisi (an early plow), taught people to till the soil, and set up the system of "holding market at midday" — from eating to healing to trade, his hand is in all of it. In the Ming and Qing dynasties, Shennong worship came to Taiwan with Hoklo and Hakka immigrants. For people who live off the land, no god is closer to home.

temples.name: Zhunan Wugu Temple
temples.deityStory: Its full name is Zhunan Toufen Zaoqiao Wugu Temple. Built in 1797 (the 2nd year of the Jiaqing reign), it is worshipped jointly by the Hoklo and Hakka communities around Zhunan and Toufen. The rear hall holds a giant statue of Shennong completed in 1993.

associatedTemples: Zhunan Wugu Temple (Zhunan Township, Miaoli County)
worship:
Offerings to Shennong are mainly flowers, fruit, cakes and tea. The most distinctive offering is the "five grains" — rice, wheat, beans, sesame and millet — symbolizing the abundance he grants. Some people also offer medicinal herbs in memory of his tasting a hundred plants.

Who comes to pray most? Farmers, around spring planting, sowing and harvest, asking for a good crop, protection from pests and escape from natural disasters. Chinese medicine doctors and herbal merchants come when opening a practice or furthering their training, praying for skill and for their patients' recovery. Each year on Shennong's birthday, herbal shops and Chinese medicine associations come to worship as a group — a highlight of the trade's calendar.

In Hakka villages such as those in Miaoli, the Shennong temple is the spiritual center of the community, and the birthday festival combines Hakka opera with traditional food. Worship the god, then watch the show — that's the most Hakka day of the year.
festivals:
**Shennong's Holy Birthday**: the 26th day of the 4th lunar month. Shennong temples hold grand celebrations with sutra chanting, processions, banquets and Hakka opera performances.

**Spring Planting Blessings**: after Lunar New Year (around the 15th day of the 1st lunar month), farmers and people in farm-related trades come to Shennong temples to pray for a good year's harvest — one of the most important rites of Taiwan's traditional farming society.

**Autumn Harvest Thanksgiving**: around the autumn equinox (the 8th lunar month), farmers return to Shennong temples after the harvest to thank the god.

**Herbal Medicine Trade Tradition**: each year on Shennong's birthday, herbal medicine shops, Chinese medicine practitioners' associations and others visit Shennong temples together to worship — a key moment for seeing Taiwan's traditional medicine culture up close.

name: Hakka Mazu (Hakka Sea Goddess)
domain: Protection at sea, safe travels, protecting Hakka settlers
description: Mazu is a sea goddess, and the Hakka mostly live in the hills — so why do Hakka villages worship her too? Hakka Mazu, also called Tianshang Shengmu (Holy Mother in Heaven) or Mazu Po, is the distinctive form Mazu worship has taken among Taiwan's Hakka people. Hoklo Mazu temples are mostly in fishing villages and harbors, watching over those who make their living at sea; Hakka Mazu temples are mostly in settlements in the hills, watching over farming and family. One goddess, two personalities. Hakka Mazu festivals have their own character as well: sutras chanted in Hakka, music from Hakka bayin ensembles, "harvest opera" staged after the autumn harvest to thank the goddess, and temple affairs run by Hakka ancestral trusts. When Mazu came to Hakka country, she adopted its ways. Xinpu's Yutian Temple in Hsinchu — whose people brought an incense banner from Beigang Chaotian Temple in 1910 and finished the temple in 1914 — is one of the few Mazu temples in Hsinchu's Hakka region.
story:
The Hakka have guardian gods of their own — the Three Mountain Kings, the Yimin Ye, Dingguang Gufo. So why worship Mazu, the goddess of the Hoklo too?

The answer lies at sea. In the Ming and Qing dynasties, Hakka people from Tingzhou in Fujian and Meizhou in Guangdong crossed to Taiwan and faced the same waves of the Black Water Ditch as everyone else; once in Taiwan, travel back and forth across the strait meant the same sea. Mazu was the shared sea guardian of Taiwan's Han Chinese, Hoklo and Hakka alike — before boarding, the settlers all lit the same incense.

The interesting part is what happened after they came ashore. Mazu followed the Hakka into their hill settlements and slowly became Hakka herself: the rites switched to sutras chanted in Hakka, festivals were accompanied by Hakka bayin music, harvest opera was performed after the autumn harvest to thank her, temple affairs were handed to Hakka ancestral trusts, and many families even wrote Mazu into their genealogies as the family's protector.

The same Lin Moniang who rescues sailors in fishing villages became, in Hakka country, an elder watching over harvests and households. One goddess, interpreted differently by different peoples — that is one of the most fascinating things about Taiwan's immigrant society.

temples.name: Xinpu Yutian Temple
temples.deityStory: In 1910, Xinpu residents brought an incense banner from Beigang Chaotian Temple, and the temple was completed in 1914 — one of the few Mazu temples in Hsinchu's Hakka region. Every year on the 16th day of the 8th lunar month, Xinpu's eleven districts take turns hosting a Divine Pig Competition and festival.

temples.name: Tongluo Tianhou Temple
temples.deityStory: The local Mazu temple of Tongluo Township in Miaoli, a predominantly Hakka community.

associatedTemples: Xinpu Yutian Temple (Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County)
Tongluo Tianhou Temple (Tongluo Township, Miaoli County)
worship:
You can tell a Hakka Mazu altar by what's on it. Besides the usual flowers, fruit, cakes and tea, there are Hakka rice treats — mugwort rice cakes, sticky rice cake, red turtle cakes and vegetable buns — and at festivals, Hakka flat rice noodles and salty guangbing biscuits.

The rites differ too: sutras are chanted in Hakka rather than Hokkien, major festivals are accompanied by a Hakka bayin ensemble (a traditional Hakka band), and after the autumn harvest (around the 8th and 9th lunar months) comes the uniquely Hakka "harvest opera" to thank the goddess. Blessings are returned with thanks at year's end and sought anew at the start of the year, in an unbroken cycle.

Many Hakka families count Mazu as their family protector, and weddings, funerals and family gatherings all bring the whole clan to the Mazu temple. In Hakka villages, worshipping Mazu has never been a private matter — it's a family affair.
festivals:
**Hakka Mazu's Holy Birthday**: the 23rd day of the 3rd lunar month (the same day as Hoklo Mazu). Hakka Mazu temples hold celebrations that bring in Hakka opera, Hakka food and Hakka bayin music.

**Harvest Opera**: each year after the autumn harvest (the 8th to 9th lunar months), Hakka Mazu temples stage "**harvest opera**" (opera performed to thank the gods) — a uniquely Hakka tradition that blends religion and art and draws Hakka descendants who have moved away back home to watch.

**Returning and Seeking Blessings**: during "**returning blessings**" at year's end (the 12th lunar month) and "**seeking blessings**" at the start of the year (the 1st lunar month), Hakka Mazu temples are the center of collective worship for Hakka families.

**Hakka Cultural Festivals**: Hakka cultural festivals in Miaoli, Pingtung and elsewhere often partner with Hakka Mazu temples, holding Hakka opera, traditional food and cultural talks in the temple squares — a good time to see how Hakka culture is being carried forward today.

name: Dingguang Gufo (Ancient Buddha of Steady Light)
domain: Protecting Hakka settlers from Tingzhou, safe voyages, warding off disaster and bringing blessings
description: In Tamsui there is a temple with a half-moon pond dug before its gate, and for two centuries it has been both a temple and a hometown guild hall: Yinshan Temple, dedicated to Dingguang Gufo — also called Dingguang Fo or Master Dingguang — guardian of the Hakka people from Tingzhou. Dingguang Gufo was born Zheng Ziyan, a monk of the early Northern Song from Tong'an in Quanzhou. He went to Wuping in Tingzhou to teach the dharma, treat the sick and help people out of trouble, and after his death he was deified as a local guardian. When Tingzhou Hakka crossed to Taiwan in the Ming and Qing dynasties, facing malaria, epidemics and conflict, this "god from home" was their greatest spiritual support. Tamsui's Yinshan Temple, built in 1822, is the only fully preserved Qing-dynasty Tingzhou guild hall in Taiwan and a national historic site — a single building holding up both faith and homesickness, and the most tangible record of Hakka migration to Taiwan.
story:
Legend says Zheng Ziyan was born in Fujian at the end of the Five Dynasties period and became a monk at eleven. After traveling to famous mountains, he settled at Nan'an Rock in Wuping, Tingzhou, where he taught and healed for the rest of his life.

His most famous legend is the taming of a snake demon. In those days, it's said, a great serpent plagued Tingzhou — tens of zhang long, breathing poisonous mist and ruining crops. Zheng Ziyan walked to its lair himself and, without any force, subdued it through compassion alone; the serpent took refuge in the Buddha's teaching and never harmed anyone again.

Another tale is of rain. One year a great drought struck Tingzhou, the crops withered and the people were desperate. Zheng Ziyan set up an altar and prayed for rain for seven days and seven nights — and on the eighth day, the rain came. From then on he was revered as a "living Buddha whose prayers for rain are answered."

Zheng Ziyan finally passed away seated in meditation at Nan'an Rock, at the age of 82. The local people made his body into a gilded image and enshrined it, and later generations honored him as Dingguang Gufo.

Centuries later, Tingzhou Hakka crossed the sea to Taiwan and carried his incense to Tamsui, Changhua and Hsinchu. The people left home, but the god never left the people — that is the story of Dingguang Gufo in Taiwan.

temples.name: Tamsui Yinshan Temple
temples.deityStory: Yinshan Temple was begun in 1822 (the 2nd year of the Daoguang reign) with money pooled by Hakka immigrants from Tingzhou and completed in 1824 (the 4th year of Daoguang). It is the only fully preserved Qing-dynasty Tingzhou guild hall in Taiwan and a national historic site. Its architecture follows the Tingzhou tradition, unlike typical Hoklo temples, and a half-moon pond lies in front. Yinshan Temple was not only a place of worship but also the Tingzhou Hakka's guild hall of the time, serving as a place for fellow natives to gather and help one another.

associatedTemples: Tamsui Yinshan Temple (Tamsui District, New Taipei City)
worship:
Offerings to Dingguang Gufo are vegetarian: flowers, fruit, tea and cakes, and Hakka devotees often add rice treats such as mugwort rice cakes, sticky rice cake and red turtle cakes — the altar alone tells you who worships here. Chanting usually means the Heart Sutra, the Great Compassion Mantra, or the god's holy name, "Namo Dingguang Gufo."

His worship is closely tied to the Hakka calendar: "seeking blessings" for peace at the start of the year, "returning blessings" in thanks at year's end, and the celebrations and processions of his birthday (the 6th day of the 1st lunar month) — three key moments each year.

At the two historic temples, Tamsui's Yinshan Temple and Changhua's Dingguang Buddha Temple, you can still see the "ancestral trust," a Hakka form of collectively managing temple property. The temple is not just a place to pray; it is the mutual-aid network the Tingzhou Hakka have kept for two hundred years.
festivals:
**Dingguang Gufo's Holy Birthday**: the 6th day of the 1st lunar month. Dingguang Gufo temples hold grand celebrations, including sutra chanting, processions and banquets.

**Hakka Worship Traditions**: during "**returning blessings**" (year's end) and "**seeking blessings**" (start of the year), Dingguang Gufo temples are a central place of worship for the Hakka community, combining religion with Hakka culture — an important time to see how Taiwan's Hakka traditions are passed on.

**Processions**: some temples hold a procession on the god's birthday, and the areas the god passes through are considered blessed.

name: Cankui Zushi (Master of Humility)
domain: Protecting pioneer settlers, guarding the mountains and forests, blessing land clearing
description: Imagine a god whose very name means "shame." Cankui Zushi — the Patriarch of Humility, also called Zushi Gong or the Patriarch of Yinna Mountain (sometimes written Yinlin Mountain) — was Pan Liaoquan of the Tang dynasty, who attained the Way on Yinna Mountain on the Fujian–Guangdong border; his ancestral temple is Lingguang Temple on Yinna Mountain in Meixian, Guangdong. "Cankui" was his dharma name, and the popular explanation is this: in life he felt he had failed to help suffering people in time, and on his deathbed, deeply ashamed, he vowed to become a spirit after death and protect all living beings forever. Taiwan has about thirty to forty temples dedicated principally to him, mostly around Lugu and Zhongliao in Nantou, with others in Chiayi, Yunlin, Changhua and Taichung. When settlers opened up the mountains of central Taiwan, facing malaria, wild beasts and the unknown, Cankui Zushi guarded the hills and forests, drove off epidemics and protected their farming — a god pioneers relied on. Lugu Fenghuangshan Temple in Nantou, built in the Jiaqing era of the Qing dynasty, is one of the best-known Cankui Zushi temples, and the Lugu area celebrates the Patriarch's birthday on the 16th day of the 3rd lunar month.
story:
Here was a spiritual seeker who, at the end of his life, thought not about his merits but about his shortcomings.

The most widely told version goes like this: Cankui Zushi was once Pan Liaoquan, an eminent monk of the Tang dynasty, who during his years of practice failed to help suffering people in time. To everyone around him he was already a man of the Way, yet on his deathbed he blamed himself deeply and vowed to become a spirit after death, protecting all beings forever and making up for what he hadn't managed in life. And so "Cankui" — shame, humility — became his name.

Whichever version you hear, what devotees see in this god are the qualities they admire most: constant self-reflection, the courage to take responsibility, and compassion for others. A god named for shame has become a model people hold themselves to — however much you've done, you can always do better.

temples.name: Lugu Fenghuangshan Temple
temples.deityStory: Fenghuangshan Temple is one of Taiwan's best-known Cankui Zushi temples. It stands in Fenghuang Village, Lugu Township, Nantou, was built in the Jiaqing era of the Qing dynasty, and sits against the mountainside in quiet, secluded surroundings.

associatedTemples: Lugu Fenghuangshan Temple (Lugu Township, Nantou County)
worship:
Offerings to Cankui Zushi are mainly tea, fresh flowers and fruit, though some temples also accept the Three Sacrifices — worship in the mountains has always been simple and practical, and sincerity matters more than show. Devotees mostly pray for smooth progress in their work on the land, peace at home, and protection from misfortune.

The busiest time is the Patriarch's birthday. Temples around Lugu celebrate it on the 16th day of the 3rd lunar month; dates vary from temple to temple, and some mark it on the 15th day of the 4th month or the 28th day of the 10th.
festivals: The ten Patriarch temples of Lugu Township, Nantou County, jointly celebrate the birthday of Cankui Zushi of Yinna Mountain on the 16th day of the 3rd lunar month. Patriarch temples elsewhere vary in date, with some celebrating on the 15th day of the 4th lunar month or the 28th day of the 10th.
